claim: Obesity and its associated metabolic disorders, such as type two diabetes, are major public health and economic burdens around the world.
source: Obesity and its associated metabolic disorders, such as type two diabetes, are major public health and economic burdens around the world (Dobbs et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dobbs et al., 2014

claim: Exercise can be an effective lifestyle intervention to combat obesity and metabolic diseases.
source: Exercise can be an effective lifestyle intervention to combat obesity and metabolic diseases (Handschin and Spiegelman, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Handschin and Spiegelman, 2008

claim: The combined efficacy of exercise and dietary regimens on type two diabetes can surpass that of pharmacological interventions alone.
source: Moreover, the combined efficacy of exercise and dietary regimens on type two diabetes can surpass that of pharmacological interventions alone (Knowler et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Knowler et al., 2002

claim: The hypothalamus plays a key role in the central control of energy balance and glucose homeostasis.
source: The hypothalamus plays a key role in the central control of energy balance and glucose homeostasis (Gautron et al., 2015; Morton et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gautron et al., 2015 and Morton et al., 2014

claim: The ventral medial nucleus of the hypothalamus (VMH) and the orphan nuclear receptor, steroidogenic factor-1 (SF-1), are critical for the regulation of metabolism.
source: In particular, the ventral medial nucleus of the hypothalamus (VMH) and the orphan nuclear receptor, steroidogenic factor-1 (SF-1; official gene name Nr5a1) are critical for the regulation of metabolism (Cheung et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2011a; Parker et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cheung et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2011a; Parker et al., 2002

claim: Within the brain, SF-1 is expressed within the VMH.
source: Within the brain, SF-1 is expressed within the VMH and several studies have demonstrated that SF-1-expressing neurons (SF-1 neurons), and SF-1 itself, are required for adaptive responses to metabolic challenges that occur with high-fat diet (HFD) feeding (Choi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Choi et al., 2013

claim: SF-1-expressing neurons and SF-1 itself are required for adaptive responses to metabolic challenges that occur with high-fat diet feeding.
source: Within the brain, SF-1 is expressed within the VMH and several studies have demonstrated that SF-1-expressing neurons (SF-1 neurons), and SF-1 itself, are required for adaptive responses to metabolic challenges that occur with high-fat diet (HFD) feeding (Choi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Choi et al., 2013

claim: VMH-specific deletions of SF-1 and other genes such as Sirt1, Slc17a6, and Esr1 blunt the adaptive thermogenic response to HFD.
source: VMH-specific deletions of SF-1 and other genes such as Sirt1, Slc17a6, and Esr1 blunt the adaptive thermogenic response to HFD (Kim et al., 2011b; Ramadori et al., 2011; Tong et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kim et al., 2011b; Ramadori et al., 2011; Tong et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2010

claim: VMH-specific deletions of SF-1 and other genes had modest effects in chow-fed mice.
source: Interestingly, these deletions had modest effects in chow-fed mice (Choi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Choi et al., 2013

claim: Exercise training significantly increased mRNA levels of SF-1, Bdnf, Cnr1, and Crhr2 in the mediobasal hypothalamus.
source: We found that exercise training significantly increased mRNA levels of SF-1, Bdnf, Cnr1, and Crhr2 in the mediobasal hypothalamus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: SF-1 expression is restricted and includes the VMH, the anterior pituitary gland, the adrenal gland and the gonads.
source: The SF-1 expression is restricted and includes the VMH, the anterior pituitary gland, the adrenal gland and the gonads (Parker et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Parker et al., 2002

claim: SF-1 expression in the pituitary gland, adrenal gland, and the gonads is intact in VMH∆SF-1 mice.
source: Of note, SF-1 expression in the pituitary gland, adrenal gland, and the gonads is intact in VMH∆SF-1 mice (Kim et al., 2011b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2011b

claim: Deletion of SF-1 in the VMH did not affect body weight, glucose levels, oxygen consumption, or food intake in sedentary chow-fed mice.
source: Deletion of SF-1 in the VMH did not affect body weight, glucose levels, oxygen consumption, or food intake in sedentary chow-fed mice (Kim et al., 2011b) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2011b and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: VMH∆SF-1 mice exhibited significantly lower endurance-exercise capacity compared to control mice.
source: We found that VMH∆SF-1 mice exhibited significantly lower endurance-exercise capacity compared to control mice (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Cardiac function was normal in VMH∆SF-1 mice.
source: Echocardiography revealed normal cardiac function, and function of isolated mitochondria from skeletal muscle were not impaired in VMH∆SF-1 mice (Figure 1B–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-E

claim: Function of isolated mitochondria from skeletal muscle were not impaired in VMH∆SF-1 mice.
source: Echocardiography revealed normal cardiac function, and function of isolated mitochondria from skeletal muscle were not impaired in VMH∆SF-1 mice (Figure 1B–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-E

claim: Blockade of VMH neuronal activity reduces circulating free fatty acids during and after exercise.
source: Previous studies have shown that blockade of VMH neuronal activity reduces circulating free fatty acids (FFAs) during and after exercise (Miyaki et al., 2011; Scheurink et al., 1988), and FFA utilization during exercise (Miyaki et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Miyaki et al., 2011 and Scheurink et al., 1988

claim: Blockade of VMH neuronal activity reduces FFA utilization during exercise.
source: Previous studies have shown that blockade of VMH neuronal activity reduces circulating free fatty acids (FFAs) during and after exercise (Miyaki et al., 2011; Scheurink et al., 1988), and FFA utilization during exercise (Miyaki et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Miyaki et al., 2011

claim: FFAs are a critical energy resource for endurance exercise.
source: FFAs are a critical energy resource for endurance exercise (Horowitz, 2003), and disruption of FFA mobilization can impede endurance capacity (Dubé et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Horowitz, 2003

claim: Disruption of FFA mobilization can impede endurance capacity.
source: FFAs are a critical energy resource for endurance exercise (Horowitz, 2003), and disruption of FFA mobilization can impede endurance capacity (Dubé et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dubé et al., 2015

claim: FFAs between control and VMH∆SF-1 mice were comparable in sedentary mice.
source: FFAs between control and VMH∆SF-1 mice were comparable in sedentary mice (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G

claim: Several species of circulating FFAs in VMH∆SF-1 mice were significantly lower following a single exercise bout.
source: In contrast, several species of circulating FFAs in VMH∆SF-1 mice were significantly lower (Figure 1H) following a single exercise bout (15 m/min for 60 min, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H

claim: VMH∆SF-1 mice have an impaired mobilization of FFAs in response to exercise.
source: These data suggest that VMH∆SF-1 mice have an impaired mobilization of FFAs in response to exercise, which may contribute to their reduced endurance capacity.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on FFA levels after exercise

claim: Impaired mobilization of FFAs may contribute to reduced endurance capacity in VMH∆SF-1 mice.
source: These data suggest that VMH∆SF-1 mice have an impaired mobilization of FFAs in response to exercise, which may contribute to their reduced endurance capacity.
evidence: Speculative connection between FFA mobilization and endurance capacity

claim: Exercise training improves body composition by reducing fat mass and increasing (or maintaining) lean mass.
source: Exercise training improves body composition by reducing fat mass and increasing (or maintaining) lean mass (Egan and Zierath, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Egan and Zierath, 2013

claim: Exercise training significantly attenuated HFD-induced obesity in both VMH∆SF-1 and control mice as compared to sedentary mice.
source: Compared to sedentary mice, we found that exercise training significantly attenuated HFD-induced obesity in both VMH∆SF-1 and control mice as compared to sedentary mice (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B

claim: Exercised-VMH∆SF-1 mice displayed impaired improvements in body weight and body composition and displayed greater adiposity versus exercised-control mice.
source: However, exercised-VMH∆SF-1 mice displayed impaired improvements in body weight and body composition and displayed greater adiposity versus exercised-control mice (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-E

claim: Control mice had significant reductions in circulating glucose levels following training.
source: Following training, control mice also had significant reductions in circulating glucose levels. This effect was attenuated in exercised-VMH∆SF-1 mice (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F

claim: The reduction in circulating glucose levels following training was attenuated in exercised-VMH∆SF-1 mice.
source: Following training, control mice also had significant reductions in circulating glucose levels. This effect was attenuated in exercised-VMH∆SF-1 mice (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F

claim: Exercise training can increase energy expenditure in adult rodents.
source: Exercise training can increase energy expenditure in adult rodents (He et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to He et al., 2012

claim: Exercise training increased resting oxygen consumption in controls following the last bout of exercise.
source: Exercise training increased resting oxygen consumption in controls following the last bout of exercise. This response was blunted in VMH∆SF-1 mice (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-C

claim: The increase in resting oxygen consumption following exercise training was blunted in VMH∆SF-1 mice.
source: Exercise training increased resting oxygen consumption in controls following the last bout of exercise. This response was blunted in VMH∆SF-1 mice (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-C

claim: Training-induced increases in heat production were blunted in VMH∆SF-1 mice.
source: In line with the lack of an increase in oxygen consumption, training-induced increases in heat production were blunted in VMH∆SF-1 mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Changes in body weight were comparable between exercised-VMH∆SF-1 and exercised control mice.
source: Changes in body weight (Figure 3D and E), water intake and ambulatory movement (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) were comparable between exercised-VMH∆SF-1 and exercised control mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D, E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Water intake was comparable between exercised-VMH∆SF-1 and exercised control mice.
source: Changes in body weight (Figure 3D and E), water intake and ambulatory movement (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) were comparable between exercised-VMH∆SF-1 and exercised control mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Ambulatory movement was comparable between exercised-VMH∆SF-1 and exercised control mice.
source: Changes in body weight (Figure 3D and E), water intake and ambulatory movement (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) were comparable between exercised-VMH∆SF-1 and exercised control mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Exercise training altered respiratory exchange ratio and food intake in control mice, but not in VMH∆SF-1 mice.
source: We found that exercise training altered respiratory exchange ratio and food intake in control mice, but not in VMH∆SF-1 mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D

claim: The loss of SF-1 in the VMH blunts exercise-induced increases in oxygen consumption.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that the loss of SF-1 in the VMH blunts exercise-induced increases in oxygen consumption, and consequently attenuates exercise-induced reductions in fat mass.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on oxygen consumption and fat mass

claim: The loss of SF-1 in the VMH attenuates exercise-induced reductions in fat mass.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that the loss of SF-1 in the VMH blunts exercise-induced increases in oxygen consumption, and consequently attenuates exercise-induced reductions in fat mass.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on oxygen consumption and fat mass

claim: Lean mass is correlated with resting metabolic rate.
source: Many studies have shown that lean mass is correlated with resting metabolic rate (Müller et al., 2002; Tschöp et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Müller et al., 2002 and Tschöp et al., 2012

claim: Lean mass was significantly correlated with oxygen consumption in all genotypes.
source: While lean mass was significantly correlated with oxygen consumption in all genotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), we unexpectedly found that exercised-VMH∆SF-1 mice had significantly less lean mass compared to exercised-control mice (Figure 3F–H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: Exercised-VMH∆SF-1 mice had significantly less lean mass compared to exercised-control mice.
source: While lean mass was significantly correlated with oxygen consumption in all genotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), we unexpectedly found that exercised-VMH∆SF-1 mice had significantly less lean mass compared to exercised-control mice (Figure 3F–H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F-H

claim: The reduction in lean mass may underlie the failure of VMH∆SF-1 mice to increase energy expenditure in response to exercise.
source: These results suggest that the reduction in lean mass may underlie the failure of VMH∆SF-1 mice to increase energy expenditure in response to exercise.
evidence: Inferred from correlation between lean mass and energy expenditure

claim: Exercise training increased relative skeletal muscle mass in control mice.
source: Predictably, we found that exercise-induced increases in relative skeletal muscle mass (Figure 4A–D) in control mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-D

claim: The improvements in relative skeletal muscle mass were impaired in VMH∆SF-1 mice compared to control mice.
source: The improvements in relative skeletal muscle mass (Figure 4A–D), body composition, and circulating glucose levels were impaired in VMH∆SF-1 mice compared to control mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The improvements in body composition were impaired in VMH∆SF-1 mice compared to control mice.
source: The improvements in relative skeletal muscle mass (Figure 4A–D), body composition, and circulating glucose levels were impaired in VMH∆SF-1 mice compared to control mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The improvements in circulating glucose levels were impaired in VMH∆SF-1 mice compared to control mice.
source: The improvements in relative skeletal muscle mass (Figure 4A–D), body composition, and circulating glucose levels were impaired in VMH∆SF-1 mice compared to control mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The VMH regulates the sympathetic nervous system.
source: A number of studies have demonstrated that the VMH regulates the sympathetic nervous system (SNS) (King, 2006; Niijima et al., 1984), including altering substrate utilization by skeletal muscle (Haque et al., 1999; Shiuchi et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to King, 2006; Niijima et al., 1984; Haque et al., 1999; Shiuchi et al., 2009

claim: The VMH alters substrate utilization by skeletal muscle.
source: A number of studies have demonstrated that the VMH regulates the sympathetic nervous system (SNS) (King, 2006; Niijima et al., 1984), including altering substrate utilization by skeletal muscle (Haque et al., 1999; Shiuchi et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Haque et al., 1999 and Shiuchi et al., 2009

claim: Circulating levels of norepinephrine, glucagon and insulin were not significantly different between control and VMH∆SF-1 mice following a single bout of exercise.
source: Circulating levels of norepinephrine, glucagon and insulin were not significantly different between groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B-D

claim: Circulating epinephrine levels in exercised-VMH∆SF-1 mice were significantly lower than those of exercised-control mice.
source: Notably, circulating epinephrine levels in exercised-VMH∆SF-1 mice were significantly lower than those of exercised-control mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A

claim: A single bout of exercise increased Th pre-mRNA levels in the adrenal gland of control mice.
source: Interestingly, a single bout of exercise increased Th pre-mRNA levels in the adrenal gland of control mice. In contrast, deletion of SF-1 in the VMH blunted these responses (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E

claim: Deletion of SF-1 in the VMH blunted the exercise-induced increase in Th pre-mRNA levels in the adrenal gland.
source: Interestingly, a single bout of exercise increased Th pre-mRNA levels in the adrenal gland of control mice. In contrast, deletion of SF-1 in the VMH blunted these responses (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E

claim: Sympathetic nervous system activation in response to exercise is blunted in VMH∆SF-1 mice.
source: These data are consistent with the model that sympathetic nervous system activation in response to exercise is blunted in VMH∆SF-1 mice.
evidence: Inferred from data on catecholamines and Th pre-mRNA levels

claim: Pharmacological stimulation of β2-adrenergic receptor can increase skeletal muscle mass by both promoting protein synthesis and suppressing protein degradation.
source: Pharmacological stimulation of β2-adrenergic receptor (β2AdR, the major isoform in skeletal muscle) can increase skeletal muscle mass by both promoting protein synthesis and suppressing protein degradation (Lynch and Ryall, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lynch and Ryall, 2008

claim: β2AdR stimulation increases skeletal muscle mass, which are predominantly composed of fast-twitch fibers.
source: Notably, β2AdR stimulation increases skeletal muscle mass, which are predominantly composed of fast-twitch fibers (Lynch and Ryall, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lynch and Ryall, 2008

claim: Deletion of SF-1 in the VMH affected the size of the tibialis anterior (TA), gastrocnemius and the extensor digitorum longus (EDL) muscles.
source: Interestingly, deletion of SF-1 in the VMH affected the size of the tibialis anterior (TA), gastrocnemius and the extensor digitorum longus (EDL) muscles (Figure 4B-D) which are predominantly composed of fast-twitch fibers in mice (Diffee et al., 2002; Taylor et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B-D and citations to Diffee et al., 2002 and Taylor et al., 2008

claim: The TA, gastrocnemius and EDL muscles are predominantly composed of fast-twitch fibers in mice.
source: Interestingly, deletion of SF-1 in the VMH affected the size of the tibialis anterior (TA), gastrocnemius and the extensor digitorum longus (EDL) muscles (Figure 4B-D) which are predominantly composed of fast-twitch fibers in mice (Diffee et al., 2002; Taylor et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Diffee et al., 2002 and Taylor et al., 2008

claim: Treatment with a β2AdR agonist leads to phosphorylation of cAMP response element binding protein (pCREB).
source: Treatment with a β2AdR agonist leads to phosphorylation of cAMP response element binding protein (pCREB) (Koopman et al., 2010; Lynch and Ryall, 2008), which can bind to the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma co-activator 1-alpha (PGC-1α; Ppargc1a) promoter to regulate various transcriptional events (Fernandez-Marcos and Auwerx, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Koopman et al., 2010 and Lynch and Ryall, 2008

claim: pCREB can bind to the PGC-1α promoter to regulate various transcriptional events.
source: Treatment with a β2AdR agonist leads to phosphorylation of cAMP response element binding protein (pCREB) (Koopman et al., 2010; Lynch and Ryall, 2008), which can bind to the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma co-activator 1-alpha (PGC-1α; Ppargc1a) promoter to regulate various transcriptional events (Fernandez-Marcos and Auwerx, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fernandez-Marcos and Auwerx, 2011

claim: The β2AdR-pCREB-PGC-1α pathway is thought to contribute to the numerous adaptive responses to exercise.
source: This pathway is thought to contribute to the numerous adaptive responses to exercise (Handschin and Spiegelman, 2008) including altered protein synthesis and degradation (Bruno et al., 2014; Ruas et al., 2012; Sandri et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Handschin and Spiegelman, 2008; Bruno et al., 2014; Ruas et al., 2012; Sandri et al., 2006

claim: The β2AdR-pCREB-PGC-1α pathway contributes to altered protein synthesis and degradation in response to exercise.
source: This pathway is thought to contribute to the numerous adaptive responses to exercise (Handschin and Spiegelman, 2008) including altered protein synthesis and degradation (Bruno et al., 2014; Ruas et al., 2012; Sandri et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bruno et al., 2014; Ruas et al., 2012; Sandri et al., 2006

claim: Training adaptations are the cumulative effect of multiple individual exercise bouts.
source: As training adaptations are the cumulative effect of multiple individual exercise bouts (Hawley et al., 2014), we focused instead on the effect of a single bout of exercise (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B) on skeletal muscle signaling pathways.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hawley et al., 2014

claim: SF-1 deletion in the VMH blunted phosphorylation of CREB in skeletal muscle following acute exercise.
source: We found that SF-1 deletion in the VMH blunted phosphorylation of CREB (pCREB) in skeletal muscle following acute exercise (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E

claim: Skeletal muscle mRNA levels of the adrenergic receptor subtypes did not differ between control and VMH∆SF-1 mice.
source: However, skeletal muscle mRNA levels of the adrenergic receptor (AdR) subtypes did not differ between control and VMH∆SF-1 mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: The mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) signaling pathway regulates protein synthesis/degradation and can be activated by β2AdR signaling.
source: The mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) signaling pathway regulates protein synthesis/degradation and can be activated by β2AdR signaling (Lynch and Ryall, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lynch and Ryall, 2008

claim: Phosphorylated proteins in the mTOR pathway were comparable between exercised-control and -VMH∆SF-1 mice.
source: Phosphorylated proteins in the mTOR pathway were comparable between exercised-control and -VMH∆SF-1 mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A-D

claim: Phosphorylation of AKT, ACC and AMPK were comparable between control and VMH∆SF-1 mice.
source: Moreover, phosphorylation of AKT, ACC and AMPK were also comparable between control and VMH∆SF-1 mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 4E–H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4E-H

claim: The mRNA levels of Nr4a2, Crem, Foxo1, and Smad3 were not statistically different between control and VMH∆SF-1 mice.
source: Additionally, Nr4a2, Crem, Foxo1, and Smad3, which are known to be altered by catecholamines (Viguerie et al., 2004), β2AdR-agonist injection (Pearen et al., 2009), and exercise (Catoire et al., 2012; Egan et al., 2013). However, the mRNA levels of these genes were not statistically different between control and VMH∆SF-1 mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5A-D

claim: Control mice showed a significant increase in mRNA expression of total Ppargc1a and each of the Ppargc1a isoforms after acute exercise.
source: As expected, control mice showed a significant increase in mRNA expression of total Ppargc1a and each of the Ppargc1a isoforms, including Ppargc1a-4, after acute exercise (Figure 4F–J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F-J

claim: Exercise-induced expression of total Ppargc1a and Ppargc1a-2 in muscle was blunted in VMH∆SF-1 mice.
source: We found that exercise-induced expression of total Ppargc1a and Ppargc1a-2 in muscle was blunted in VMH∆SF-1 mice (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H

claim: PGC-1α-2 was impaired in exercised-VMH∆SF-1 mice, suggesting that the reduction in total Ppargc1a expression levels is due to changes in Ppargc1a-2.
source: PGC-1α-2 was impaired in exercised-VMH∆SF-1 mice, suggesting that the reduction in total Ppargc1a expression levels is due to changes in Ppargc1a-2 (Figure 4F).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on Ppargc1a isoforms

claim: Acute exercise did not significantly alter Myog, Myod1, Fbxo32, and Ctsl in control mice.
source: We also examined mRNA expression levels of Myog, Myod1, Fbxo32, and Ctsl, all of which regulate protein synthesis and degradation (Liu et al., 2010; Sandri et al., 2006). While acute exercise did not significantly alter these genes in control mice; exercised-VMH∆SF-1 mice had increased levels of Myog and Fbxo32 (Figure 4—figure supplement 5E–H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5E-H

claim: Exercised-VMH∆SF-1 mice had increased levels of Myog and Fbxo32.
source: We also examined mRNA expression levels of Myog, Myod1, Fbxo32, and Ctsl, all of which regulate protein synthesis and degradation (Liu et al., 2010; Sandri et al., 2006). While acute exercise did not significantly alter these genes in control mice; exercised-VMH∆SF-1 mice had increased levels of Myog and Fbxo32 (Figure 4—figure supplement 5E–H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5E-H

claim: Deletion of SF-1 in the VMH may affect protein turnover in the skeletal muscle in response to exercise.
source: These findings suggest that deletion of SF-1 in the VMH may affect protein turnover in the skeletal muscle in response to exercise.
evidence: Inferred from data on genes regulating protein synthesis and degradation

claim: PGC-1α-2 may be important for regulating protein turnover in response to sympathetic input from the CNS following exercise.
source: While the physiological role of PGC-1α-2 is still unclear, we speculate that it may be important for regulating protein turnover in response to sympathetic input from the CNS following exercise.
evidence: Speculative statement about the role of PGC-1α-2

claim: SF-1 in the VMH is required for metabolic adaptations.
source: Our current results coupled with previous observations (Choi et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2011b; Ramadori et al., 2011; Tong et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2010) suggest that SF-1 in the VMH is required for metabolic adaptations.
evidence: Inferred from current and previous studies

claim: SF-1 in the VMH is required for the metabolic adaptations to exercise training, including increasing metabolic rate, skeletal muscle mass, and decreased adiposity.
source: In particular, our date supports a model predicting that SF-1 in the VMH is required for the metabolic adaptations to exercise training, including increasing metabolic rate, skeletal muscle mass, and decreased adiposity.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data in the study

claim: Stimulation of the VMH enhances lipolysis in white adipose tissues and facilitates fatty acid oxidation.
source: For example, stimulation of the VMH enhances lipolysis in white adipose tissues and facilitates fatty acid oxidation (Ruffin and Nicolaidis, 1999; Takahashi and Shimazu, 1981).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ruffin and Nicolaidis, 1999 and Takahashi and Shimazu, 1981

claim: Blockade of β-adrenergic receptors in the VMH impedes the increase in circulating fatty acids during exercise.
source: Blockade of β-adrenergic receptors (βAdRs) in the VMH impedes the increase in circulating fatty acids during exercise (Scheurink et al., 1988).
evidence: Supported by citation to Scheurink et al., 1988

claim: Microinjections of the anesthetic lidocaine or βAdR antagonists into the VMH inhibits fatty acid oxidation during exercise.
source: Moreover, microinjections of the anesthetic lidocaine or βAdR antagonists into the VMH inhibits fatty acid oxidation during exercise (Miyaki et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Miyaki et al., 2011

claim: Suppression of neuronal activity in the VMH apparently does not affect metabolism under sedentary conditions.
source: Of note, suppression of neuronal activity in the VMH apparently does not affect metabolism under sedentary conditions (Miyaki et al., 2011; Takahashi and Shimazu, 1981).
evidence: Supported by citations to Miyaki et al., 2011 and Takahashi and Shimazu, 1981

claim: SF-1 in the VMH is required for the full adaptive response to exercise training.
source: Collectively, our findings indicate that SF-1 in the VMH is required for the full adaptive response to exercise training.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data in the study

claim: The VMH regulates the SNS in order to enhance lipolysis, fatty acid oxidation, and glucose uptake in peripheral tissues.
source: A large body of literature suggests that the VMH regulates the SNS in order to enhance lipolysis, fatty acid oxidation, and glucose uptake in peripheral tissues (Adler et al., 2012; Bamshad et al., 1999; Haque et al., 1999; King, 2006; Minokoshi et al., 1999; Niijima et al., 1984; Perkins et al., 1981; Sakaguchi and Bray, 1987a, 1987b; Sakaguchi et al., 1988; Takahashi and Shimazu, 1981, 1982).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Microinjection of leptin or orexin into the VMH increases glucose uptake in skeletal muscle via the SNS.
source: For instance, microinjection of leptin or orexin into the VMH increases glucose uptake in skeletal muscle via the SNS (Haque et al., 1999; Shiuchi et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Haque et al., 1999 and Shiuchi et al., 2009

claim: SF-1 neurons project to regions of the brain that control activity of the autonomic nervous system including the parabrachial nucleus, nucleus of the solitary tract and the rostral ventrolateral medulla.
source: Although the precise circuitry downstream of the VMH remains to be determined, genetic tracing has revealed that SF-1 neurons project to regions of the brain that control activity of the autonomic nervous system including the parabrachial nucleus, nucleus of the solitary tract and the rostral ventrolateral medulla (Lindberg et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lindberg et al., 2013

claim: Optogenetic photostimulation of SF-1 neurons rapidly alters heart rate.
source: Interestingly, a recent study demonstrated that optogenetic photostimulation of SF-1 neurons rapidly alters heart rate (Wang et al., 2015), further suggesting that SF-1 may regulate autonomic function.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2015

claim: SF-1 neurons act on the SNS to regulate metabolism in the skeletal muscle and other peripheral tissues.
